sense: existing as an idea, not as a thing

terms.gloss: what is grasped by the mind (as against what can be seen and touched)
terms.grammar: phrase: a relative clause, in the number and gender of the thing meant (quae intelleguntur)
evidence: Cic. Top. 26–27: earum rērum quae sunt … earum quae intelleguntur
terms.comment: Classical Latin has no adjective for “abstract”. Cicero sets things that can be seen and touched (quae cernī tangīque possunt: a farm, a house, a wall) against things that cannot be touched or pointed to but are seen by the mind and understood (quae … cernī tamen animō atque intellegī possunt: guardianship, kinship), “under which there lies no body” (quārum rērum nūllum subest quasi corpus, Top. 27). Say so with a relative clause.

evidence: Isid. Orig. 2.24.14: quantitās abstracta (Lewis & Short, s.v. abstrahō)
terms.comment: The word of the later philosophers and grammarians, and of the modern languages; classically only the participle of abstrahō, “dragged away”.

phrases.latin: Nōn esse rūrsus ea dīcō quae tangī dēmōnstrārīve nōn possunt, cernī tamen animō atque intellegī possunt
phrases.english: Those things, on the other hand, I call non-existent which cannot be touched or pointed out, but can still be seen by the mind and understood

sources: Lewis & Short: abstraho · Lewis & Short: intellego
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. abstract.
Cicero, Topica 26–27 (ed. Wilkins, 1902), checked against the Perseus Latin texts.
